title: Thinking Loop v6: elimination and verification

D0.outcome: Explains elimination (refute candidates one at a time) and verification (check the survivor from the opponent's side) as two separate steps.

D1.outcome: From four candidates, eliminates two with a concrete refutation each and states what remains to be verified for the other two.

D2.outcome: Verifies the chosen line a second time from the opponent's side before moving, and finds the hidden flaw in positions where the first-choice line has one.

D3.outcome: In long forcing variations, records the tree, avoids rechecking, and states a reason for stopping where he stops.

D4.outcome: In own games, review notes show elimination and verification steps in critical moments with prompts off, and the rate of moves that fail verification falls over time.

misconceptions: Verifying is the same as calculating again in the same order.
A line that is calculated to the end needs no check of the first move.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S2; docs/council-synthesis.md CD-3 (one versioned Thinking Loop)
docs/first-hours.md session 4 (threat check as loop v1)
docs/council-synthesis.md Round 3 (Aagaard: elimination); sources/sheets/emlasker_common-sense.md §4.16 (do not trust an unverified perpetual)
conditions: The first-choice line must be checked from the other side; the same-order recheck repeats the same blind spot.
Applies when the decision is critical and the cost of error is high.
condition_sources: CNC CD-3 T6+ elimination and verification
contrasts: Rechecking the same variation in the same order and finding the same result (thinking inertia).
Assuming a perpetual exists without testing the king's escape squares.
Positions with a single legal move.
